.SHORT TERM...
(This afternoon through Sunday)
Issued at 243 PM EDT Sat Oct 10 2026

Post Tropical Cyclone Isaias continues to push northward into 
northern Alabama and Tennessee with lingering effects continuing 
over portions of Georgia. The main area we are watching is the 
southeast Georgia area where there is a tornado watch in effect for 
Emmanuel, Toombs, and Jefferson counties. There is a lingering band 
oriented from north to south through this area into south Georgia 
that is an area of enhanced CAPE (3000J/kg) and shear south of the 
warm front. There are multiple circulations we will continue to 
watch along this band for tornado potential through the next couple 
of hours. Further west and north, we can see the warm front boundary 
draped along I-20 that has steadily pushed north through the late 
morning/early afternoon. Areas east of I-75 and south of I-20 will 
be where we will be watching for the potential redevelopment of 
banding. All the ingredients are there to give us an elevated 
tornado and heavy rain threat BUT it will be a matter of IF this 
band can redevelop. With clearing ongoing, leaning towards at least 
some redevelopment here in the next couple of hours and lasting 
through late evening. 

Winds have begun to diminish as Isaias has moved northward which has 
resulted in the cancellation of portions of the High wind warning 
and areas of the wind advisory. Wind gusts should remain in the 20-
30mph range through the remainder of the evening with gusts in the 
higher elevations up to 40 to 50mph still possible.
Will continue to evaluate and potentially cancel early if needed.

The flood watch remains in effect through 8am tomorrow for eastern 
Georgia but will also likely be cancelled early. Areas south and 
east of I-85 in the south metro did receive anywhere from 2-4inches 
of rainfall through this morning and areas of east Georgia will 
continue to see heavy rainfall within these bands that could produce 
additional amounts of 1-3".

Isaias quickly moves northward with rain bands exiting the area 
around midnight tonight with clearing skies by tomorrow.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Monday morning through next Friday)
Issued at 243 PM EDT Sat Oct 10 2026

No changes were made to the longterm forecast.

The long term picks up after the remnants of Isaias are not but a 
memory. Dry air will settle in across the southeast and bring back a 
little bit of summer on the backside. Highs in the mid to upper 80s 
are expected as high pressure keeps winds out of the west. Drier 
conditions will start off the long term, but as the high slowly 
meanders to the east, we'll start to see a moisture return by the 
middle part of the work week brining afternoon heat index values 
back into the 90s. 

Expect overnight lows to be comfortably in the 50s and 60s for much 
of the area with winds becoming light and variable during the 
overnight hours. By next weekend, some of the model runs are 
beginning to indicate the possibility for a strong cold front to 
push down from the north that will bring fall back into the region. 
But for the meantime, enjoy a little bit more late summer and plenty 
of sunshine.

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Pleasant conditions through Sunday morning.  
Rain arrives Sunday afternoon and lasts through the night.

Pleasant and dry conditions continue through a good portion of
Sunday, with partly cloudy skies and low winds through tonight. 
Expecting to see some radiational cooling tonight with calm
winds, but light cloud cover will limit just how far
temperatures will drop. Overnight lows likely bottom out in
lower 40s for most, upper 30s in the higher elevations.

Attention then turns to Sunday afternoon and evening as the
remnants of Hurricane Isaias make their way north and east with 
the jet stream. As it exits off the DelMarVa coast and enter our
waters south of the Islands, it's expected to strengthen and
pass north of the 40/70 benchmark. PWATs will likely surge to
near 2.0", mostly along the south coast, Cape, and Islands. With 
rain arriving Sunday afternoon (early PM for the interior, later
PM for RI and eastern MA) and lingering into Monday, rainfall 
totals will likely be in the 0.75 inch to 1.0 inch range. It's 
possible some heavier rain bands set up, but confidence is low 
on where or when exactly those could develop; therefore, some 
areas could see local higher rainfall totals... possibly up to 
1.5 inches across the south coast, Cape, and Islands. 
Thankfully, the bulk of the LLJ will be kept aloft and offshore,
so the worst of the winds will be kept offshore and on the 
order of 23 to 30 knots.

KEY MESSAGE 2...The next quick moving round of rain comes 
Sunday afternoon and evening, continuing overnight and exiting 
Monday morning.

Low pressure slowly moves away from southern New England 
Monday. This will gradually bring an end to our showers from 
northwest to southeast. Still some disagreement on how quickly 
it all ends. The GFS remains on the more progressive side of the
solution envelope. The most likely area for showers to linger 
longer will be towards the Cape and islands. Further adjustments
to the timing are possible with later forecasts.

Our region then has a brief drier period Monday night into 
Tuesday morning. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...Quick round of rain around mid week, then dry 
weather returns by Thursday. 

Our region should then get clipped by a pair of low pressures, 
each taking a different track. The first should pass from the 
Great Lakes across northern New England Tuesday into Tuesday 
night. The risk for showers arrives across northern MA during 
the morning, then gradually moves south Tuesday night as the 
associated cold front approaches. Drying out Wednesday as this 
front finally moves farther offshore during the day.

High pressure over eastern Canada should briefly take over our 
weather Wednesday night into Thursday night.

The forecast for next Friday and Saturday is uncertain. A low 
pressure moving east across Canada could swing its associated 
fronts across our region during this time. The issue continues 
to be one of timing. This low pressure is quite distant from 
southern New England. Thinking a slower onset timing is more 
likely to develop with later forecasts given a high pressure 
over the North Atlantic. Then there is the question of how 
quickly it dries out on Saturday. We should see a period of 
showers some time Friday into Saturday.

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 128 PM CDT Sat Oct 10 2026

It's an awfully warm and pleasant Saturday out there for the 
second week of October. Temperatures early this afternoon are in
the upper 70s to lower 80s with a comfortable southerly breeze.
Largely sunny skies are being filtered by blowoff cirrus from 
post-tropical storm Isaias as it spins northward over the 
southeast US. The blowoff will remain overhead into the night 
and gradually retreat from west to east during the day tomorrow.
The NBM has now backed off on any mentionable PoPs in our east 
and southeast from this remnant storm for tonight and tomorrow 
morning. A few pieces of deterministic guidance, as well as a 
handful of members from various ensembles, still suggest a brief
light shower may be possible. Accordingly, maintained some 
"silent" (less than 15%) PoPs in our east in the gridded 
forecast.

Tomorrow should see highs ranging from the lower to middle 70s 
in our east to near 80 in our west and southwest. It's worth 
noting that afternoon temperatures from the NBM in the Sunday 
through Tuesday period are being skewed by a warm GEPS suite, so
have collaborated with neighboring offices to bring temps down 
closer to most other guidance. Being on the southern flank of a 
passing low on Monday, efficient warm advection driven by gusty 
southerly winds will pull highs into the 80s, possibly even 
nearing 90 closer to central IL. Near-record-breaking values are
forecast at Chicago and Rockford. Tuesday will feature a good 
spread in temps across the area with a cold frontal passage 
during the day and should range from the 70s north into the 80s 
south. High temperatures are then favored to fall through the 
rest of the week and conditions by next weekend should feel much
more like what we normally expect for the middle of October.

Still eyeing a signal for a surface low to track across the 
upper Midwest and drag a cold front across the area late Monday 
into Tuesday. Recently, however, global guidance has backed off 
a bit on PoPs with the better forcing and moisture favored just 
to our north and northeast ahead of the low and a weakly-forced,
moisture-starved cold front as it moves across on Tuesday. A 
low chance for some showers and perhaps a thunderstorm still 
exists late Monday and into Tuesday, and should be maximized 
around our northeastern CWA. Regular chances for rain are then 
in the forecast from late Tuesday into Friday as the regional 
synoptic pattern becomes a bit more active for next week.

.SHORT TERM...
(This evening through Sunday)
Issued at 1208 PM CDT Sat Oct 10 2026

Despite today's cool, pleasant morning lows, temperatures will once 
again climb well above average into the upper 80s to low 90s this 
afternoon due to a mid-level ridge axis overhead and dry, sunny 
conditions. Tonight, increasing southerly flow will begin to 
return low-level Gulf moisture to North and Central TX. As a 
result, Sunday's morning lows should be a few degrees higher than
today. Winds will become breezy tomorrow afternoon as the 
pressure gradient over our area tightens and boundary layer mixing
brings gusty winds to the surface. Sunday's high temps will be 
similar to today given the continued influence of the ridge and 
efficient mixing. No precipitation is expected in the short term 
period. 

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Sunday night through next Friday)
Issued at 132 PM CDT Sat Oct 10 2026

Gulf moisture will continue to stream into Texas early next week, 
and with additional moisture aloft moving in from the Pacific on 
Monday, PW values should rise to 1.8-2 inches, indicating an 
anomalously moist environment for this time of year. Low-level 
moisture advection has a 10-20% chance of producing some isolated 
precip in the Brazos valley each afternoon Monday and Tuesday, but 
the vast majority across our area will remain dry due to a nearby 
mid-level ridge. As the ridge strengthens and moves overhead 
Tuesday and Wednesday, temperatures will be on an upward trend, 
reaching the low-to-mid 90s during the day and falling only into 
the 70s at night.

Ensemble guidance has maintained the mid-to-late week signal for 
rain chances across the Southern Plains as an upper-level trough 
axis is expected to progress east of the Rockies, bringing at least 
weak forcing for ascent to the region. However, uncertainty has 
increased since yesterday in the progression of the trough and its 
associated cold front. The GEFS suite, AI-GFS, and EC-AIFS 
continue to favor a more progressive trough, which almost all 
guidance backed yesterday. This solution would bring the front in 
earlier, likely on Friday, and would cause a greater drop in 
temps. About one third of LREF members, mostly ENS, have trended 
slower with the trough, delaying frontal passage until the weekend
and keeping milder post-frontal temps. The 12Z deterministic Euro
even has the front stalling in Central TX. Full frontal passage 
still appears more likely at this time, but we'll be monitoring 
for trends in the guidance over the coming days.

As a result, our confidence is higher that the front will bring
notably cooler temps to North TX compared to Central TX. 
Regardless, we are confident that high moisture content and 
sufficient instability for precipitation will be in place midweek,
particularly near the Red River, where these ingredients may
overlap with modest shear to produce a few organized 
thunderstorms and locally heavy rainfall. At this time, the best 
rain chances appear to be Wednesday evening through Friday morning
(or the arrival of the front). Should the front be delayed or 
even stall out in Central TX, rain chances may extend into next 
weekend.

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Remnants of Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias to 
bring rain, breezy to windy conditions, and the threat of 
tornadoes Sunday.

Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias continues to lift northward across
Georgia and Alabama. This system has weakened considerably after
last evening's landfall while losing all tropical
characteristics. The associated mid-level circulation 
strengthens and becomes a large cutoff low later tonight. To the
east, surface high pressure over the northeastern U.S. today 
moves offshore off southern New England tonight.

In advance of this broad area of low pressure, a thick high
cirrus shield continues to expand north and east into the Great
Lakes and New England. While this system still looms well to the
southwest of the area, some light scattered showers continue to
lift across I-64 toward the I-66 corridor. However, any amounts
are very light with some radar returns not even reaching the
ground. The thick cloud cover will hold temperatures mainly in
the upper 60s to low 70s this afternoon.

Looking ahead, the interaction of Isaias' remnants to the west 
and surface high to the east will create a large area of 
convergence / broad frontal zone over the Mid-Atlantic. There is
good model agreement that rain steadily moves from south to 
north this evening into tonight as forcing for ascent increases 
with some mid-level height falls in response to the approaching 
cutoff low. It will take a bit of time for the surface to truly
saturate, so any rainfall this afternoon to evening across 
central Virginia will struggle to amount to much. Eventually, 
tropical moisture with PWATs at or above 2" surges in after 
midnight. 

It is worth mentioning again that conditions are favorable for a 
widespread soaking rain, and 12Z and 00Z models have responded 
with more QPF across the region. Forcing for ascent increases 
tonight, and especially Sunday morning into Sunday afternoon as 
mid-level heights fall with the approach of the cutoff low. 
Enhanced low-level convergence and moisture transport will peak
Sunday morning into early Sunday afternoon. Strengthening 
easterly flow into the Blue Ridge could also produce enhanced 
rain amounts due to orographic effects. As a result, forecast 
rain amounts have increased to 2.0-3.0", with locally higher 
amounts of 3-5" possible. With this uptick, Flood Watches were
issued across the Blue Ridge eastward into the central Virginia
Piedmont region. This is in effect on Sunday 5 AM until Monday 2
AM. Some eastward expansion may be necessary if models trends
hold on or show further upticks.

Another noticeable trend in recent guidance is the higher 
probabilities for severe weather Sunday afternoon. The main 
synoptically forced rain moves north of the area early Sunday 
afternoon. Rapid height falls and increasing low-level winds 
provide a few hour window where some breaks in the clouds area 
possible, leading to pockets of instability. A surface wave of 
low pressure moves right through the area Sunday afternoon. 
Forecast soundings indicate large, cyclonic hodographs, with 
ample shear in place to support organized severe convection. 
Clusters of thunderstorms develop along the leading edge of the 
surface low pressure, with tornadoes and damaging wind gusts as 
the main threats (looks mostly to be east of the Blue Ridge). 
The NAM12, RRFS, and 12Z HRRR all show this scenario. The big 
question still remains how much instability actually develops. 
SPC has maintained a Slight Risk for Sunday, with a recent northward
expansion to just south of I-66 in Virginia.

The strong mid-level circulation is going to bring windy conditions 
to the Alleghenies and Blue Ridge, starting late tonight into Sunday 
morning. Wind Advisories were issued for downsloping easterly 
winds in the Alleghenies (western Garrett, western Grant, and 
western Pendleton Counties), and the Blue Ridge. The current 
forecast for peak wind gusts is 40-50 mph in the 
Alleghenies/Blue Ridge and 20-30 mph elsewhere.

The remnants of Isaias push offshore Monday, bringing an end to any 
lingering showers. While conditions return humid and warm Monday, 
there likely will not be much in the way of shower activity due
to subsidence behind the departing trough.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Above normal temperatures Tuesday will fall the 
second half of the week as moisture starved fronts move through.

Brief ridging in the wake of the tropical remnants may bring high 
temperatures Tuesday to near 80 degrees. Low pressure passing north 
of the area will send a cold front southward Tuesday night. Most of 
the rain likely remains across Pennsylvania, although some showers 
may sneak southward. Showers will also be possible along the 
Allegheny Front. There's still some significant model spread on the 
progression of this front during the middle of the week, with a 
large spread of temperatures possible on Wednesday. However, the 
general trend will be downward for the second half of the week. A 
wave of low pressure or cold front may approach toward the end of 
the week which could bring some rain, but model spread remains high 
on the details.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z SUNDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...
VFR conditions prevail through this evening, then conditions 
deteriorate tonight into Sunday as the remnants of Post-
Tropical Cyclone Isaias impact the region. IFR conditions are 
likely to overspread all terminals late tonight through Sunday 
afternoon, as periods of rain and gusty winds cross the region. 
There could be a few hour period of thunderstorms Sunday 
afternoon, some of which could be severe, though this threat is 
greatest east of the Blue Ridge. Have introduced the potential
for thunderstorms as a PROB30 group at KDCA, KIAD, and KBWI. 
Conditions improve Monday morning, with the return of VFR 
conditions. Northwest winds gusting around 20-25 knots possible 
Monday afternoon. Winds eventually return to southerly by
Tuesday ahead of the next system.

Prevailing VFR conditions are anticipated from Tuesday through 
Thursday. A passing cold front could bring some showers and 
reduced CIGs Thursday night into Friday. Southwesterly winds 
shift northerly by Thursday morning, then flow easterly later 
Thursday evening.

&&

.MARINE...
Marine conditions are expected to deteriorate tonight through Sunday 
night as the remnants of Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias move 
across the Mid-Atlantic. SCA conditions develop this evening in
the central Chesapeake Bay, then across all the waters tonight.
The strongest winds, gusts around 30 to 35 knots, will occur 
Sunday morning. In particular, the uptick is most pronounced
over the more southern waters where Gale Warnings have been
introduced from 5 AM until 11 AM Sunday. Special Marine 
Warnings may be needed Sunday afternoon for thunderstorms 
capable of producing strong wind gusts and waterspouts. The 
remnants of Isaias move offshore Monday morning, but SCA 
conditions continue through Monday evening due to gusty 
northwest winds in its wake.

Winds could fluctuate in & out of SCA criteria between Wednesday and

Widespread tidal flooding is likely during the Sunday afternoon to

.DISCUSSION /Through Saturday/...
Issued at 112 PM MDT Sat Oct 10 2026

Radar shows light showers across the higher terrain at this hour.
Today will continue our streak of above-average days with high 
temperatures in the 80s for the plains. SW flow aloft has 
increased over the last 24 hours. Thus, winds could be breezy in 
our mountains and the eastern plains this afternoon. With relative
humidity dropping into the teens across the eastern plains, we 
expect a few hours of elevated to near-critical fire weather 
conditions for those locations this afternoon. Some isolated to 
scattered showers will continue to remain possible in the higher 
terrain today, with a low (~10-20%) chance for these to push off 
into the urban corridor and the adjacent plains. Little measurable
rainfall is expected and this would only be widely scattered in 
the higher terrain. Some showers could continue through the 
overnight for far western portions of our area including Jackson, 
Grand, and Summit counties. Given increasing high-level cloud 
cover overnight, it will be another unseasonably warm night with 
another record warm minimum for the day possible. 57 degrees 
(1881) is the record warm minimum for Sunday.

On Sunday, the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel move into the 
western US with any notable precipitation staying well to the west 
of our forecast area. For our area, high temperatures should take a 
slight dip, but will remain in the 80s for most of the plains. 
Another round of isolated to scattered showers will be possible for 
the high country, mainly west of the Continental Divide. The 
forecast starts to become more uncertain by Monday. It is becoming 
more likely that a backdoor cold front will stall somewhere 
over/just north our northeastern counties. South of the front, 
temperatures should stay in the upper 70s to near 80, but north of 
the front, temperatures could drop into the low 70s. Regardless, we 
expect this front to push through the area by Tuesday morning 
bringing a "cool" down with highs into the upper 60s to low 70s on 
the plains (except for our far southeastern counties) for Tuesday 
afternoon- still a few degrees above average for this time of year.

There are still significant differences in the forecast across the 
latest model suite starting Tuesday night through the end of the 
week. The position/speed/strength of the trough and upper-level 
low(s) remains uncertain. The ECMWF has trended slower and further 
west over the last few runs while the GFS moves a somewhat weaker 
low over or north of our area. In general, we expect PoPs to 
increase starting late Tuesday and peak on Wednesday with Thursday 
continuing to trend drier. Note that a vast majority of ensemble 
members (~90%) give Denver some measurable rainfall, with amounts 
generally under 1/2 inch. Some of the moisture associated with the 
remnants of Hurricane Simon could be pulled into the flow aloft, 
mainly affecting areas to our east. As snow levels drop through the 
week and moisture increases, the mountains and high country (mainly 
above 10,000 feet) could see a few inches of snow. Our northern 
mountains in particular look most favorable.

From Thursday onward, the GFS progresses the upper-level low off to 
the east with another low moving from Canada into the Great Lakes 
region towards the end of the week and into the weekend. The ECMWF 
keeps the upper-level low hung up over the Four Corners through the 
end of the week. Regardless, high temperatures look to finally stay 
near to below average through at least next Saturday with at least 
some low PoPs in the mix.

.SHORT TERM (SAT-TUE)...10/755 PM.

The most significant impacts over the short term will be COASTAL
FLOODING RISKS. Please refer to Beaches section below as well as 
CFWLOX for further details on coastal flooding issues.

Tropical Storm Rachel is still forecast to track well south of 
Los Angeles. A pair of low pressure systems will drop from the
north and interact with moisture from Rachel. This will result in
below normal temperatures through Tuesday, as well as periods of
light to moderate rain through Monday. Chances are highest on
Sunday for the southern portion of our four county area, but 
widespread accumulating rain is very likely everywhere on Monday.
Minor rain impacts are expected, focused the slick roads that
might have some isolated spots of minor flooding. The one
exception is the San Gabriel Mountains. While the heart of the
deep tropical moisture plume from Rachel will stay east of Los
Angeles County, several model projections wobble enough of the
edge of the plume to produce 1-2 inches of rain on Sunday over the
San Gabriels, with peak hourly rates around 0.5 inches per hour.
This would be enough to cause some concerns from a mudslide or two
in the mountain roads and canyons, as well as producing shallow
debris flows over the Summit burn scar. This is something to keep
and eye on. 

As far as rainfall amounts are concerned, it appears the majority
of our rainfall totals will come from the "first" system from 
late tonight into Sunday afternoon. Further details on the rain 
are below.

We are also expecting fairly breezy conditions for much of
southwest California, especially in the mountains and deserts of
eastern Los Angeles County. There will be a very sharp uptick in
onshore pressure gradients Sunday morning along with the upper
level influence of the second upper low dropping down south. A 
wind advisory has been issued for the San Gabriel Mountains as 
well as the Antelope Valley for Sunday, with gustiest winds 
expected during the afternoon through late evening hours. 

Otherwise, much cooler temps will bring a relief to many after a
long stretch of very hot weather.

Some details to note:

       be 150-300% of normal.
     - PWATs will decrease on Monday.

       through Monday.

            inches over the San Gabriel Mountains (locally 3.00).
          - Ventura County: generally 0.10-0.50 inches with
            locally higher amounts possible over the mountains.
          - SBA/SLO Counties: generally under 0.25 inches.

       up to around 0.50"/hour will be possible for LA County.

Hurricane Isaias, is forecast to slide across the Mid-Atlantic 
region Sunday night into early Monday morning. As this occurs, it is 
forecast to weaken further with the closed mid level low opening up 
more into a trough. The main impacts for our area will be widespread 
rainfall and some gusty winds.

Large scale ascent will start to increase from the south late 
tonight as the system approaches. An east to southeast robust low-
level jet (around 925 mb) on the order of 40-60 knots will 
overspread our area Sunday morning and this will rapidly increase 
the warm air advection initially above a marine stable layer. This 
will enhance the lift (strong 700-850 mb frontogenesis) as the low 
to mid level flow veers with height. In addition, deeper moisture 
will be advected northward into our area with this peaking Sunday 
afternoon into the evening as a warm sector gradually advects 
northward. The precipitable water values are forecast to quickly 
increase from south to north late tonight through Sunday to 1.75-
2.25 inches. As this coincides with strong forcing for ascent 
Sunday, some periods of heavier rain should occur. Total rainfall 
amounts still look to be 1-2 inches across the entire area, however 
up to 3 inches will be possible where some enhancement and/or 
embedded convective elements occur. This event should initially be 
in the form of stratiform rain before transitioning to more 
convective/showery Sunday night into early Monday morning. WPC has 
maintained most of the region in a Marginal Risk (level 1 out of 4) 
for excessive rainfall for Sunday into Sunday night, which means 
isolated instances of flash flooding will be possible. There are 
currently no river gauges forecast to reach minor flood stage, 
however if even heavier rain occurs into northern NJ (especially 
2.5+ inches), this could cause some gauges in the Raritan basin (the 
Millstone River) to rise to minor flood stage. If rainfall rates 
become high enough for a time, then some urban/roadway flooding will 
also be possible.

As the low-level jet moves across the area and the warm sector 
gradually spreads northward on Sunday, an easterly wind will 
increase and become gusty. Where the better warm sector gets, the 
surface winds will veer more out of the southeast to south with 
time. The surface wind speeds will be driven by how much mixing 
occurs within the boundary layer, and this looks to be greatest 
along the coast given the onshore wind and warmer ocean allowing for 
a bit more mixing onto the adjacent land. There is a robust wind 
field forecast to be in place not to far above the surface, however 
a moist/stable layer should keep this from fully mixing down. Wind 
gusts up to 30 mph are anticipated inland with gusts up to 40 mph 
along the coast. The winds should diminish Sunday night as the 
remnant surface low slides across our area and the low-level jet 
shifts away from our region.

While this is the remnants of a tropical system, it has had plenty 
of time being a post-tropical system prior to reach our area. 
Nevertheless, low-level shear profiles increase quite a bit for a 
time Sunday into Sunday evening. For awhile there will be a marine 
influence given the onshore flow and with a period of stratiform 
rain this will keep the instability limited to near zero. However, 
as the main rain shield starts to shift north and east of our area 
either later Sunday afternoon and/or Sunday evening, some 
instability may try to advect northward across Delmarva into 
southern New Jersey especially. Model forecast soundings show the 
flow veering with time and this would weaken the low-level 
shear/helicity (spin). There appears to be a very small window of 
opportunity though in Delmarva where lingering stronger deep-layer 
shear overlaps with some increase in instability for perhaps a few 
transient low-topped supercells with an isolated damaging wind gust 
possible. The severe scenario however is highly contingent on how 
much higher dew points advect northward with enough low-level 
instability, and this looks to be greater to our south and 
southwest. The risk for a weak/brief tornado in our area is 
therefore very low.

Some showers linger early Monday morning, especially from about the 
I-95 corridor on south and east, then drying should quickly occur 
during Monday as a north to northwest wind increases for a time and 
the entire weakening system exits to our east and northeast.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Minor tidal flooding possible with Sunday morning's
high tide, mainly for coastal areas within Delaware Bay. A Coastal
Flood Advisory is in effect for Kent County, DE. 

With a period of east/southeasterly flow expected and the 
upcoming New Moon, increased tidal levels are expected later

tidal flooding, mainly for coastal communities along Delaware

This won't be a significant event for the Atlantic Ocean coastline,

The eastern side of Delaware Bay in NJ and northern part of the

The current forecast has no tidal flooding for areas along the

.KEY MESSAGES...

- An unsettled weather pattern will prevail throughout the 
  weekend as the remnants of Tropical Cyclone Rachel move into the
  southwest United States, resulting in heightened chances for 
  showers and thunderstorms, widespread gusty winds on Sunday, and
  much cooler temperatures.

- Rain chances will continue for portions of the region, 
  especially across South Central Arizona, early next week along 
  with well-below normal temperatures. 

- A drier and quieter weather pattern is expected by the middle 
  and latter portion of next week along with gradually warming 
  temperatures. 


&&

.SHORT TERM /TODAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
An expansive area of abundant midlevel moisture has spread into the 
Southwestern US ahead of Tropical Storm Rachel, which can be seen in 
midlevel water vapor imagery quickly ejecting northeastward towards 
Northern Baja. A subtropical cutoff low intensifying to its west, 
well offshore, is also apparent and leading to an intenifying jet 
streak downstream. The combination of abundant midlevel moisture and 
upper level diffluence hes led to fairly widespread elevated showers 
and scattered thunderstorms across Southwest AZ and Southeast CA so 
far. Locally strong wind gusts and transient linear organization 
have been observed with some of these storms, despite the weak 
instability (RAP analyzed MLCAPE no more than 500 J/kg). Inverted-V 
GFS bufr soundings and DCAPE upwards of 1000 J/kg across much of the 
forecast area will mean that even weak storms are capable of wind 
gusts upwards of 35-50 mph and kicking up at least localized blowing 
dust, as was observed in Gila Bend late this morning. This activity 
will continue to push north and east with time, reaching portions of 
the Greater Phoenix Area over the next hour or so. 

A window of time with an environment supportive of more robust and 
potentially organized convection is still expected to arrive late 
tonight into Sunday morning, as better low-level moisture with the 
arrival of Rachel will support briefly higher instability upwards of 
500-1000 J/kg of MUCAPE. The higher instability combined with 
vertical wind shear in excess of 40 kts will support a severe 
threat, with SPC highlighting much of the area under a marginal 
risk. Damaging wind gusts will be the main threat, however, with low-
level shear increasing above 20 kts along with 0-3 km Storm Relative 
Helicity over 100-200 m2/s2, there will be a non-zero threat for a 
brief tornado or two. 

Perhaps the most widespread impact from the arrival of the remnants 
of Rachel will be gusty winds. Guidance is still in excellent 
agreement that the intensifying jet downstream from the cutoff low 
and remnant low/circulation of Rachel will support 850 mb southerly 
flow upwards of 40 kts near/just east of the Lower Colorado River 
Sunday morning. This is in excess of climatological maximum wind 
speeds at 850 mb for this time of year. Additionally, a dry slot 
behind the remnant Rachel circulation may add to the wind threat, as 
there will be additional mixing through the BL during the Day on 
Sunday, helping tap the higher momentum air aloft. As a result, 
expect fairly windespread gusts upwards of 35-45 mph across the 
forecast area Sunday, with locally higher speeds upwards of 50-60 
mph (especially over higher terrain). Wind gusts this high could 
certainty result in areas of blowing dust in the dust prone areas. 
As the remnants of Rachel move northward into southern Nevada by 
late Sunday afternoon/early evening, winds will weaken as the 
gradient weakens.

In terms of rainfall amounts, given that much of the activity will 
be mostly scattered in nature, event-total rainfall amounts across 
much of the area will be under 0.75" with the potential that some 
areas see next to nothing. However, there can be some locally higher 
amounts in excess of 1" in areas that see a training of convection. 
The more favorable area for more widespread activity will be mainly 
across Joshua Tree National Park, close to where Rachel will track, 
and thus the potential will exist for more widespread amounts in 
excess of 1" with a Flood Watch in effect from this evening through 
Sunday afternoon.

Tempertures across the area will decrease over the weekend, with 
lower desert highs this afternoon about 10 degrees cooler compared 
to Friday and readings in the low to mid 90s. The more abundant 
cloud cover as well as rainfall activity will cause temperatures to 
cool another 7-10 degrees on Sunday as afternoon highs only reach 
the low to middle 80s.

&&

.LONG TERM /MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/... 
Unsettled weather will continue through early next week as the large-
scale trough that will settle across the west coast over the weekend 
will gradually migrate eastward. The associated large-scale forcing 
for ascent combined with ample low-level moisture will support 
scattered showers and embedded thunderstorms during the day, mainly 
across the foothills and higher terrain areas north and east of 
Phoenix in upslope flow. Thereafter, as the main cold front 
associated with the trough moves through late Monday night into 
Tuesday morning, there will likely be a band of showers with 
embedded thunderstorms that moves through, particularly across south-
central AZ, before rain chances end by Tuesday afternoon/evening as 
drier air filters in. At this point any of the rain that falls early 
next week will generally be of the nuisance type. Quieter weather
with near zero rain chances can be expected starting Wednesday 
and will persist through the end of the week.

With the presence of the trough as well as more abundant cloud 
cover, well-below normal temperatures are expected during the first 
half of the week with many of the lower desert locations likely 
staying in the 70s for afternoon highs. Early morning lows will also 
be below normal with the coolest morning expected on Wednesday when 
many areas are expected to drop into the 50s with even some 40s 
across the higher terrain areas. Temperatures will then gradually 
rebound into the 80s by the latter portion of the week.

&&

.AVIATION...Updated at 1920Z.

South Central Arizona including KPHX, KIWA, KSDL, and KDVT:

Scattered showers and storms, strong winds, and potential
slantwise visibility reductions are all in the forecast through
the next 24 hours. Confidence in timing of everything in the
latest TAF package is low to moderate. Showers and storms will be
possible at just about any time, but with odds slightly better
this afternoon through tonight and Sunday morning. SE winds are
expected to veer SW this afternoon and then eventually back SE-E
this evening, but wind directions may become variable this evening 
based on shower and storm activity. Storms will be capable of
generating strong wind gusts and blowing dust. The most impactful
time period will likely be Sunday morning between 14-19Z when a 
band of showers and storms are forecast to move through with lower
CIGs down to 4-5K ft AGL and southerly wind gusts up to 30kt.
Beginning with and following the band of rain, S-SW winds up to
15-20 kts and gusting up to 30-35 kts is expected through the 
afternoon, which may lead to a lot of lofted dust and reduce 
slantwise visibility.

Southeast California/Southwest Arizona including KIPL and KBLH:

Periods of SHRA with the potential for isolated TSRA along with 
erratic wind directions and strong wind gusts will be the main 
weather issues as thick midlevel cigs develop over the area. Winds
will favor an E/SE component through tonight and then eventually
S/SW by late Sunday morning. VCSH/VCTS chances will exist at both
terminals through this afternoon and evening before drying. Very
strong S/SE winds are expected Sunday morning, especially between
10-16Z with sustained speeds around 15-25 kts and gusts as high as
35-45 kts. There is some uncertainty if the stronger gusts will
fully materialize in the morning, but winds will be strong enough
regardless to generate blowing dust and impact slantwise
visibility.

&&

.FIRE WEATHER...
A much more unsettled weather pattern has taken shape this 
weekend as increasing moisture associated with the remnants of 
Tropical Storm Rachel brings increasing rain chances. Chances for
wetting rain will continue to increase through Sunday morning  
with a greater than 50-70% chance of wetting rainfall area wide. 
Winds will also increase significantly, especially late tonight 
through Sunday with widespread gusts exceeding 30-40 mph. With the
increasing moisture and cooler temperatures, MinRH values will 
increase from 25-40% today to 45-70% on Sunday along with good to 
excellent overnight recoveries. Another weather system will bring 
additional chances for wetting rainfall early next week, mainly 
for the foothills and higher terrain of the eastern districts, 
before quieter weather settles in by the middle of the week. 
Temperatures will steadily cool this weekend, with well-below 
normal temperatures expected for the first half of the next week.

morning, and a Frost Advisory remains in effect for most areas

Columbia. While the majority of the precipitation is expected to

coast and over higher terrain. The decaying atmospheric river 
system is set to shift southward late Tuesday into Wednesday, 
bringing increasing chances for rain across western Washington. 
However, the path of the atmospheric river remains fairly 
uncertain at this time, with many ensemble members keeping 
western Washington on the dry side.

A high pressure ridge will then build into the Pacific Northwest
on Thursday as another atmospheric river system traverses well
to the north. This will bring a few days of warming and drying,
with low level offshore flow and highs reaching the lower 70s by
Friday. Some uncertainty remains over how long the high pressure
will remain in place, with potential for troughing to break down

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 138 PM EDT Sat Oct 10 2026

*** BREEZY WITH RAIN SHOWERS THROUGH SUNDAY ***

The remnants of Isaias are bringing portions of southern and central 
Kentucky beneficial rain early Saturday afternoon, while winds 
steadily increase out of the east-northeast. Thankfully, gusts have 
generally stayed in the 20-30 mph range so far, though a few have 
reached 35 mph just to our south in central Tennessee - running on 
the low end of HREF guidance as is often the case in warm advection 
regimes characterized by stable low levels. Given a notable LLJ - 
evident via 50-55 kt winds at just 1kft AGL off of HPX's VAD - 
lifting north across the area this evening, there remains a low 
chance that momentum transfer via heavier showers could mix down a 
rogue 40+ mph gust, but Bufkit soundings from various models suggest 
this would be brief and localized, with the risk decreasing sharply 
after 7-8pm EDT as the low level inversion strengthens. Hence, we 
don't anticipate needing a Wind Advisory at this time, but opted to 
continue the Special Weather Statement (SPS) through 7pm EDT 
mentioning the low chance of minor impacts like lightweight, outdoor 
objects blowing around.

Otherwise, scattered showers will continue overnight, with perhaps a 
rumble of thunder or two this evening as MUCAPE, just barely poking 
into the dendritic growth zone (DGZ) for charge separation, reaches 
300-500 J/kg - highest over the Bluegrass. We'll keep an extra eye 
on radar during the evening, but the chance for severe weather is 
exceptionally low.

The surface low will pivot over eastern Kentucky tomorrow, resulting 
in lingering showers mainly over the Bluegrass. Though we may see a 
few peaks of sunshine during the afternoon mainly west of I-65, the 
low will have "filled" (weakened) considerably by that time so winds 
will be relatively light. This position of the low to our east 
should also reduce the risk for cold air funnels and/or a landspout, 
with the RAP/NAM both showing highest (>1) non-supercell tornado 
parameters (NSTs) in far eastern Kentucky and parts of West 
Virginia, though our risk remains nonzero. Any showers will be slow-
moving, so there could be some localized pockets of moderate-heavy 
rainfall (again, most likely over the Bluegrass) exceeding 1.5 
inches, but this is not anticipated to cause any hydrological 
impacts given 6 hour Flash Flood Guidance (FFG), or the minimum 
amount of rainfall required to cause flooding, is running 3-4 inches 
due to the dry antecedent conditions. Due to the showery nature of 
the precipitation this evening and again tomorrow afternoon, 
rainfall totals will vary considerably from one location to another. 
HREF/NBM 10th-90th percentile ranges for storm totals span less than 
a quarter inch to more than 2 in spots, with high end amounts 
running highest over the Bluegrass. Rain should finally taper off 
tomorrow evening as dry air works in from the northwest behind the 
low. High temperatures tomorrow will, like today, struggle to 
surpass 70, which is near normal for mid October.

*** DRY MONDAY-TUESDAY, RAIN CHANCES RETURN MIDWEEK ***

We may kick off the work week with some fog early Monday morning if 
clouds break up, since surface high pressure will be over the area 
resulting in light winds. The 12z HRRR is certainly advertising the 
potential with sub quarter-mile visibilities near/east of the I-75 
corridor. We'll monitor trends in cloud cover and winds to reassess 
that potential, but for now we'll hold off on a key message about 
the fog, which has been added to the gridded forecast east of 
roughly I-65. Global models and their ensembles are in agreement 
that ridging will build back over the Ohio Valley on Monday, with 
southwest surface winds and deep mixing bringing temperatures back 
into the mid 80s during the afternoon - about 15 degrees warmer than 
Sunday. Tuesday will be similarly warm, though becoming less dry as 
Gulf moisture, lifted into the Plains on Monday, slowly spills into 
our area from the west. The GFS and ECMWF then each depict a 
southern stream shortwave ejecting out of the Southern/Central 
Plains and into the Illinois/Indiana sometime Wednesday into 
Thursday, which forecast soundings suggest will result in some 
elevated instability and (conditional on a trigger) some chance for 
showers and thunderstorms. At this time, the National Blend of 
Models (NBM) gives the area a 20-40% chance for rain Wednesday into 
Thursday. The jury's out on how things will evolve at the end of the 
week, with EOF patterns (specifically PC1 for EOF1) for 500mb height 
suggesting model spread in the depth of troughing over the Upper 
Midwest/Great Lakes is the primary driver of uncertainty during the 
Friday-Saturday timeframe. This may be related to the deterministic 
models, which have portrayed various outcomes with potential 
interaction between a cutoff low over the Four Corners and a series 
of systems rippling through the northern stream jet.

Monday through Saturday:

Oblong low pressure spanning from the High Plains to the

yields some low chances (~10-20%) for showers in the daytime hours

drifting overhead at some point this weekend. This should lead to
strong CAA, much colder temperatures, and frost potential for our

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...
The remnants of Isaias will trek across the area beginning 
tonight, and lasting through Monday morning. It will likely 
bring rain and some winds with it. 

The first impacts from wind will ramp up in the Pennsylvania
ridges into tonight as low pressure approaches from the 
southwest. This will force ridge- perpendicular south-easterlies
in the Laurel Mountains and high terrain of West Virgina, with 
most recent model guidance having the ridgetops gusting upwards 
of 40mph after 8pm as flow accelerates up and over the Laurel 
Highlands. 

Overnight, the low will approach and the sfc-850mb layer is 
expected to stabilize around the ridge-lines, which is expected
to both accelerate flow at the ridgetops as high as 45mph to 
55mph, but also make thermodynamic profiles more conducive for 
downsloping immediately west of the Laurel Mountains (with 
gusts up to 45mph to 55mph most possible for eastern suburbs of 
Morgantown, Uniontown, Connellsville, eastern suburbs of Mount 
Pleasant, and Derry). There is still a question of if this 
occurs or not based on the exact thermodynamics, but though the
risk was prudent enough to upgrade, particularly with the 
worst- case scenario of winds near Uniontown of 60mph. The old 
wind advisory encompassed all high terrain. Lowland zones were 
added in Westmoreland, Fayette, and Monongalia, but in reality,
the gustiest winds will be fairly confined to the aforementioned
areas. 

Into Sunday, the low will depart and surface profiles will
become less stable in the sfc-850mb layer, making both synoptic
and downslope wind less likely by the 11am to 2pm window. This
is also the end time for the wind advisory.

Rain amounts, and the location of heaviest rain have become 
more confident. Downsloping effects within and roughly 50 miles
west of the ridges will actually tamper rain amounts, with most
likely totals less than 0.75" in western PA and northern WV,
with a worst-case scenario of 1.25". 

Rainfall amounts will likely be more widespread into eastern 
Ohio and parts of northwest PA with the absence of downslope 
effects and the warm conveyor belt wrapping around the north-
side of the low and a region of mid-level frontogenesis and 
generalized ascent. Even then, rainfall amounts are most likely 
in the range of 1" to 1.75", with worst-case localized amounts 
of up to 2" to 3". Hires guidance continues to hint at the 
potential for a narrow axis of up to 2" in 6hr, but even then 
those amounts are still below flash flood guidance given the 
extended dry period. Nonetheless, areal flooding where rain is 
maximized is possible, but low probability. Occasional urban 
issues and leaves clogging storm drains may occur.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
There is increasing confidence of an eastern trough into late-
week. While there is still notable timing and amplitude
uncertainty, another chance of some gusty winds and will need to
be monitored, along with a cooler temperatures. A higher-
amplitude, more western trough axis scenario could bring the 
highest impacts via winds or even the chance of the first 
snowflakes of the season via lake-enhancement. Though there are
still numerous, lower impact scenarios (including a lower
amplitude or more eastern trough axis).

&&

As of 00z, light rain from the remnants of Isaias have begun
overspreading the area. VFR conditions are likely to initally

frequent breaks into the afternoon. Rain will ease from west to 
east Sunday afternoon/early evening, but IFR ceilings and 
possible fog will continue through the overnight with a surface 
inversion.

LBE and MGW are the most likely to keep ceilings above IFR 
during the day as enhanced easterly downsloping winds along the
ridge-line mix in some dry air. Sunday morning, winds gusts 
will likely range between 20kts-30kts with higher gusts near 
LBE/MGW (up to 30kts-40kts). Wind will begin to ease between 18Z
and 23Z. LLWS is expected overnight with the strong 40-45kt

.PREV DISCUSSION...
Issued at 336 PM EDT Wed Oct 7 2026

DISCUSSION...

Pretty quiet forecast heading through the end of the work week as 
the energetic jet stream resides mostly across Canada. Stacked low 
centered over Hudson Bay today will send a trough down through the 
Great Lakes on the nose of a mid level jet streak tonight. This 
opens the door for broad troughing to encompass a portion of the 
northern Great Lakes while high pressure slides through the Midwest 
into the Ohio Valley building a stable airmass across the southern 
Great Lakes. For tonight, northwesterly cool flow over the 
relatively warm lakes will provide a boost to instability and though 
moisture is weak, PWATs roughly 0.6 inches, there could be enough 
concentrated moisture in the region of steeper low/mid level lapse 
rates to allow some scattered showers or even a thunderstorm over 
the north half of Lake Huron. Further south into the Thumb, moisture 
is even thinner and forcing weaker, but the cool airmass and low 
level jet could be enough to touch off some scattered showers over 
the Thumb this evening into tonight. Current radar over the U.P. 
does have thunderstorms present adding to the confidence of weak 
storms over northern Huron later. 

High pressure then expands back northward across the region ending 
any rain chances Thursday into Friday. Cool air within the trough 
will drop 850mb temps into the single digits above 0C leading to 
cool highs in the 60s to end the week. Clearing skies under the 
ridge with the cool airmass in place could allow some low temps to 
fall into the upper 30s Thursday night in some of the cooler spots, 
otherwise low 40s could be in store for most locations. 

Brief but strong warm up on Saturday as strong ridging over the 
Plains advances eastward over the Great Lakes. ECMWF is a touch 
warmer (~18C at 850mb) than GFS (-16C) Saturday with strong 
southwesterly flow into the region. Current forecast is for temps to 
touch 80F in the Saginaw Valley with upper 70s for most other 
locations. The warm front leading the way could touch off a few 
showers after 00Z Saturday with the bubble of stronger theta e 
lifting through the area. Though model output is not strong in 
producing rain, we've see these leading theta e gradients on 
elevated warm fronts produce narrow brief areas of showers many 
times. For now, we'll note it and see if we need to add POPs later. 

This warmup will be brief as attention the turns to TS Isaias which 
is set to make landfall over MS Friday evening then getting drawn 
northward into the Ohio Valley before getting caught in the 
westerlies and forced to the east coast. This brings the rain shield 
into Lower MI Saturday night and/or Sunday. Details will come 
together in the coming days, but for now expect a gradient of rain 
from south to north with the highest totals over southern lower MI. 
Abundant moisture with a tropical system will lead to efficient rain 
production for any areas that get clipped by the rain shield.

MARINE...

Moderate southwesterly winds gradually weaken this evening as a cold 
front extending from low pressure near James Bay crosses the central 
Great Lakes. The lighter gradient winds also veer west-northwesterly 
behind the front early tonight. However, an uptick in speeds returns 
late tonight or early Wednesday as the upper level jet deepens over 
the region. Stability trends lower with the slightly cooler airmass, 
and given the rejuvenated low-level jet winds, mixing likely 
delivers some elevated gusts. Potential exists for gusts to around 
30 knots over portions of Lake Huron Thursday afternoon, with 
marginal gusts to gales possible for northern Huron. A Small Craft 
Advisory may be needed over The Thumb should confidence rise in the 
frequency of 25+ knot gusts, but any higher end gusts further north 
should be infrequent enough to preclude a Gale Warning. Mid/Upper 
Mississippi Valley high pressure then expands into the area Thursday 
night and Friday offering weaker winds with a southerly shift.

GOES satellite imagery shows a near ghostly remnants of what is left 
of TC Rachel being absorbed into the 568dm H5 low off the 
northern Baja Peninsula. Abundant moisture is being pushed into 
the Desert Southwest from SoCal to AZ, and into southern NV and 
UT. Some light showers are trying to reach into western NM this 
morning, but will not have more appreciable coverage until later 
this afternoon. Increasing steering flow will also keep these 
scattered showers with embedded thunderstorms moving quickly to 
the northeast. Gusty winds and a quick period of light to moderate
rainfall will be the most common hazards associated with these 
passing cells. 

Precipitation chances slide back west as the by then fully fused 
remnant trough of Rachel ejects northward toward another deep large 
scale synoptic troughing pattern digging down the west coast. Much 
of the upper level energy and associated large scale forcing will 
remain west of the area with some expansion of fast moving showers 
with embedded thunderstorms back east to the Rio Grande Valley and 
central mountain chain Sunday afternoon and evening. Stronger winds 
aloft will try to mix down to the surface across central and western 
NM, with widespread gusts of 25 to 45 mph expected. Convective 
downdrafts will be capable of upping those gusts to the 50 mph mark, 
mostly along and west of the Continental Divide Sunday afternoon.

(Monday through Friday)
Issued at 1222 PM MDT Sat Oct 10 2026

moving showers with embedded thunderstorms flowing northeastward 
across western NM and into the Rio Grande Valley. This continues 
through Tuesday with a notable dryslot continuing to shutdown 
precipitation chances along and east of the central mountain chain. 
Differences begin to arise amongst global numerical model suites 
with the evolution of the troughing pattern closing off either to 
one or two distinct low pressure systems over NV and CA. This 
doesn't have much impact on the forecast sensible weather conditions 
over NM through Tuesday, but does end up causing large downstream 
divergences amongst various model runs. Whichever direction the 
upper low ends up taking, the remnants of Hurricane Simon favor a 
progression over the TX Big Bend area, clipping southeastern NM 
Wednesday.

The 12Z GFS, many ensemble means and AI runs of the GFS and ECMWF 
all favor the H5 closed low opening and being more progressive 
Wednesday into Thursday, trekking eastward over CO. This setup 
features a classic Fall cold front sweeping west to east across the 
forecast area bringing cooler and drier conditions in its wake 
Wednesday night into Thursday morning. The backdoor portion of the 
cold front sweeps south and west thru eastern NM thereafter Thursday 
night into Friday, replenishing low level moisture. The currently 
less likely scenario advertised by the 00Z runs of the ECMWF and 
Canadian have the H5 low cutting off and retrograding back toward 
northern AZ or further west. This brings a surface cold front 
backing into eastern NM late week further west with higher moisture 
content behind it advecting in from the southern Great Plains. More 
widespread precipitation chances break out across mostly the central 
and eastern NM as a result in this scenario. It's a lower 
probability scenario at this time, but worth mentioning given the 
sharp change in forecast weather pattern it would bring.

The remnants of what was once TC Rachel and larger scale storm

chances, gusty winds, and moisture to western NM today through

what is now Hurricane Simon moves through the TX Big Bend area, 
clipping southeastern NM Tuesday night thru Wednesday. Northeastern 
NM is seeing stronger windier and drier conditions allowing for 
elevated conditions today and each afternoon thru Tuesday.

Thereafter, current forecast trends favor a sweeping Fall cold front 
moving thru the area west to east Wednesday into Thursday. A drop in 
temperatures to near or below average with some moisture behind a

.FORECAST UPDATE...
Issued at 955 PM EDT Sat Oct 10 2026

The numerous rain showers have spread a bit farther north and west 
than previously thought, while eastern areas have seen less. 
Adjusted PoPs to reflect this trend. 

Bands of rain will continue to rotate north and west into the area 
into the early overnight before forcing weakens and shifts south and 
east. Kept the likely or higher PoPs going through at least midnight 
before returning to chance category across the central and southern 
portions of the area, with lower PoPs elsewhere.

Instability remains east and southeast, so continued with no mention 
of thunder. Lowered wind gusts some based on latest trends seen in 
observations and guidance.

.DISCUSSION (This Evening through Saturday)...
Issued at 147 PM EDT Sat Oct 10 2026

The remnants of Hurricane Isaias will lift up the western side of 
the Appalachians through Sunday with light showers overspreading 
most of the forecast area later today through early Sunday morning. 
Upper level ridging will build in immediately as the tropical 
remnants depart...setting the stage for near record breaking warmth 
Monday and Tuesday. Rain chances will return late Tuesday into 
Thursday with the coolest air of the season so far to follow next 
weekend.

Rest of This Afternoon through Sunday Night

Mid and high level clouds associated with Isaias continue to expand 
across the region early this afternoon with the leading edge of 
light rain now into southern Indiana. Temperatures early this 
afternoon were largely in the 70s.

The primary focus in the near term remains on the remnants of Isaias 
and impacts to the area. Trends continue to shift the storm track a 
bit further to the east resulting in lower rainfall amounts for 
central Indiana with growing confidence that much of the northwest 
half may see trace amounts or nothing at best.

Drier air is already being ingested into the weakening system with 
the rain shield approaching from the south gradually diminishing in 
coverage and intensity. By far the greater concern for heavy 
rainfall will reside in the central Appalachians where a persistent 
easterly flow in the lower levels will support upslope flow and 
enhanced rainfall rates coinciding with the deeper moisture plume. 
Across the Ohio Valley...rainfall will be reliant on the remnant 
upper low as it pivots to the northeast tonight. The best chance for 
widespread light rain will come this evening into the early 
overnight and focus across the southeast half of the forecast area 
as an increase in 850mb flow pivots across eastern Kentucky into 
West Virginia and southern Ohio. An attendant band of convergence 
will promote more widespread rainfall but with the lack of deeper 
moisture...amounts will largely remain in the 0.10 to 0.25 inch 
range along and east of I-69 dropping to nothing in the northern 
Wabash Valley. Will also pull any mention of thunder for tonight 
with virtually no instability available. 

The passage of the 850mb jet to the southeast this evening will also 
aid in a period with gusts to 20-25mph focused again primarily 
across the southeast half of the forecast area. Winds will back and 
decrease overnight with any lingering rain ending shortly after 
daybreak Sunday. Lower stratus will develop late tonight and persist 
through Sunday morning as model soundings show moisture within the 
boundary layer trapped beneath an inversion. The trend will be for a 
gradual mixing out of the stratus from the west into the afternoon 
with much drier air advecting into the region as what is left of 
Isaias moves away to the east.

Temps...clouds tonight will keep much of the area in the upper 50s. 
Low level thermals support highs Sunday in the low 70s over eastern 
counties to near 80 in the Wabash Valley.

Monday Through Saturday

Broad upper level ridging will quickly reestablish across the region 
by Monday with stronger southwesterly flow developing between a 
frontal boundary over the upper Midwest and high pressure along the 
Gulf coast. Strong warm advection will commence and result in well 
above normal temperatures for Monday and Tuesday across the region. 
Highs may flirt with 90 degrees in the Wabash Valley on Monday and 
Tuesday. For KIND...record highs of 86 for both Monday and Tuesday 
will be approached. The frontal boundary over the Great Lakes will 
drift south towards the area Tuesday afternoon with the potential 
for isolated convection increasing in coverage Tuesday night into 
Wednesday as the front shifts through the forecast area and 
eventually stalls south of the Ohio River.

An increasingly amplified flow aloft driven by a deep upper low over 
the Rockies will flatten the ridge over the southeast states while 
initiating a significant pattern change for the region by late week 
into next weekend. The aforementioned boundary will remain in a 
quasi-stationary state just south of the forecast area Wednesday 
before pulling back north in response to a surface low ejecting out 
of the Rockies and upper jet phasing. Rain with embedded 
thunderstorms will increase in coverage across the Ohio Valley as a 
result Wednesday night into Thursday before a stronger cold front 
sweeps across the region late week. 

In the wake of the frontal passage...a broad upper trough will 
settle across much of the eastern half of the country as a much 
cooler airmass will overspread the region with strong cold advection 
in place. Highs primarily in the 60s on Friday may struggle to get 
to get out of the 50s over the northeast half of the forecast area 
next weekend. Confidence continues to grow in the first frost of the 
Fall for much of the area next Saturday and Sunday nights as lows 
fall into the 30s.

- High confidence in dry weather and well above normal

&&

.SHORT TERM /THROUGH MONDAY/...
Issued at 1232 PM CDT Sat Oct 10 2026

Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias currently resides over AL, with 
synoptic analysis showing weak mid-level ridging over the Great 
Lakes region and southwesterly flow aloft over our region. This
pattern is largely aiding in keeping Isaias remnants out of our
area, with high confidence in dry weather continuing through 
the short term. Temperatures as of 1230PM range in the mid to 
upper 70s over the eastern Ozarks to the mid to upper 80s 
elsewhere. As the afternoon progresses, temps are expected to 
continue climbing into the upper 80s for the majority of the 
CWA. The exception will be over portions of the eastern 
Ozarks/south- central MO where mid- to high- level clouds 
associated with Isaias continue to filter in as shown on 
satellite imagery. This should keep temperatures a few degrees 
"cooler", with highs remaining in the low 80s. 

As Isaias continue to pivot northeast towards the Tennessee/Ohio 
Valleys on Sunday, a mid-level ridge will begin to build over the 
region, raising mid-level heights and 850mb temperatures into 
the 18- 20C range. This will allow afternoon highs to climb into
the upper 80s to low 90s across the entire forecast area. 

A weak mid level shortwave trough will push through the High Plains 
on Sunday, with an associated surface low developing east of the 
Rockies. As a result, the pressure gradient will begin to tighten, 
leading to increased southwesterly winds gusting up to 25mph 
generally west of the Highway 65 corridor. Some occasional gusts up 
to 30mph will be possible (65-85% probability according to the 
HREF). With the dry airmass remaining in place, minimum relative 
humidity values are expected to drop into the 30-40% range west of 
Highway 65, and into the 25-35% range east of the highway. Despite 
the strongest winds not aligning with the driest areas, elevated 
fire danger is expected generally along/west of Highway 65. See the 
Fire Weather section below for more detailed fuel information.

&&

.LONG TERM /MONDAY NIGHT THROUGH SATURDAY/...
Issued at 1232 PM CDT Sat Oct 10 2026

The above-normal temperatures and dry airmass will continue 
into the beginning portion of the week, with afternoon highs
reaching the upper 80s to low 90s through Tuesday. Did end up
lowering highs from the NBM deterministic by a couple degrees on
Tuesday to account for some frontal boundary positioning
uncertainty. Regardless, we'll be challenging record high
temperatures through Tuesday (see Climate section below). 

The increased winds will continue on Monday, with southwesterly
gusts up to 35mph west of Highway 65 and up to 20-30mph east of
the highway. This will once again contribute to elevated fire
weather concerns, with the greatest threat east of Highway 65
where minimum RHs drop into the 25-35% range. 

Synoptically, an upper level closed low and associated trough 
will continue dropping into the Pacific Northwest region today 
before pushing southeast towards the Rockies. It's currently 
progged to ingest Tropical Storm Rachel once she makes landfall 
off the coast of CA/northern Baja Peninsula and pushes over the
desert southwest late Tuesday. Latest guidance seems to have 
slowed this system down a bit, with large spreads between the 
models regarding the systems evolution/timing leading to 
continued uncertainty. Current thinking has a cold front 
dropping south into the area late Tuesday before stalling out 
and lifting in the form of a warm front Wednesday night, with a 
secondary cold front sweeping through Friday morning, ending the
precipitation chances. Of course, there are still timing 
uncertainties. Regardless, this will bring our next chance of 
showers and storms as early as Tuesday evening/night (30-60%), 
with the highest chances (65-85%) on Wednesday before the front 
lifts northeast Thursday (30-60% pops) and precipitation ends on
Friday with the secondary front. As the previous discussion 
mentioned, this is a fairly complex forecast with many 
discrepancies. Therefore, it's still too early to get into the 
weeds of specific rainfall amounts, with details continuing to 
get ironed out in future updates.

Behind the cold frontal passage, cooler temperatures will move
in by next weekend.

Issued at 101 AM CDT Sat Oct 10 2026

A prolonged period with substantial rainfall deficits from late
Summer and into the Fall has contributed to worsening drought 
conditions across southwest Missouri and southeast Kansas. The
latest Drought Monitor valid Oct 6 showed a continued expansion
of the D3 (Extreme Drought) and an overall categorical
degradation across the fire weather forecast area. Resultant
fuel moisture indices show similar trends. Woody FM readings
between 60-70 and Herb FM values of 30-60 suggest these fuels
are cured or very dry. Combined, these produce a Growing Season
Index (GSI) of 0.1 to 0.3, indicating fuel dormancy. 
Furthermore, KBDI values greater than 600 (and in some cases 
greater than 700) also suggest fuels are near or completely 
cured. 

While Red Flag Warning (RFW) conditions are not forecast to be 
met in the next seven days, we will officially begin our fire 
weather season messaging, and headlines will be issued should 
RFW criteria be forecast from this point onward.

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Near-record warmth is expected through the first part of the
  week. 

- A stalled front brings multiple chances for showers and
  thunderstorms for the middle of the week.

- A stronger cold front brings cooler and drier weather for the
  weekend.

&&

.SHORT TERM /THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Issued at 237 PM CDT Sat Oct 10 2026

Upper ridging remains in place across the central and eastern
United States. This has led to our recent trend toward near
record heat for mid October. Isaias made landfall yesterday on 
the Gulf coast, with its remnants currently spinning near 
Birmingham, Alabama. While not close enough to provide any rain 
to our area, high level cloudiness spilling out from the top of 
the cyclone has caused a temperature gradient across our 
forecast area this afternoon. Thicker clouds in the east have 
led to temperatures 5-10 degrees cooler than yesterday, while 
further west temperatures are once again approaching 90 degrees.

Clouds from Isaias pull away to the east tonight giving way to
another clear, calm night for most. Thus expect temperatures to
fall back to around 50 degrees in the cold spots by Sunday
morning. With even less clouds from Isaias on Sunday, the heat 
returns to the entire area on Sunday afternoon. Some locations
rise 40 degrees from their morning lows up to around 90 in the
afternoon.

&&

.LONG TERM /SUNDAY NIGHT THROUGH SATURDAY/...
Issued at 237 PM CDT Sat Oct 10 2026

A trough currently moving into the Pacific Northwest will 
gradually push back on the ridge over the coming days. While the
core of the trough lingers over the West Coast, a shortwave 
trough ejecting east will help organize a cold front over the 
Central Plains, moving southeast Monday into Tuesday. Ahead of 
the front we remain firmly under the influence of the warm upper
ridge. With the addition of a southwesterly gradient wind ahead
of the approaching front we'll see temperatures tick a degree 
or two higher, especially in areas of downslope flow off the 
Ozarks. There is a moist flow off the Gulf, but it's a bit slow 
to arrive in our area on Monday, likely leading to a period of 
elevated fire danger. This is also likely to be our warmest day 
of the week, with temperatures potentially approaching all time 
October high temperature records in the mid 90s.

The front is slow to push through our area, as the driving
trough is pushing more east than south. It's presence is more
likely to be felt in northern portions of the area on Tuesday
with some cooler weather behind it. However, the southern half
will see another hot day with temperatures near 90. NBM actually
has temperatures near all time record monthly highs again on
Tuesday, but this is on the extreme end of what's possible. 
Moisture should be increasing, with dewpoints approaching daily 
record values near 70. It takes more energy to heat moist air 
than dry air, so it will be harder to get as hot on Tuesday. 
Add in a greater potential for cloud cover near the front, and 
uncertainty on the speed of the front itself, and a more likely 
forecast at this point is for the low 90s.

The front loses its push south and lingers over our area for a
couple of days. Meanwhile, shortwave troughs continue ejecting
east over the top of the remaining ridge, leading to multiple
rounds of showers and thunderstorms in the vicinity of that
front. The main periods look to be Tuesday night into Wednesday
and then again Wednesday night into Thursday. The severe weather
potential from this activity looks low at this point as wind
shear is weak to moderate and much of the thunderstorm activity
will be elevated. However, some locally heavy rain will be
possible considering the anomalous moisture near the boundary 
(PW near climatological maximums for the time of year), the 
general track of storms east along the boundary, and the 
potential for multiple rounds.

Guidance sources are generally in good agreement on the timing
of the kicker front that comes in Thursday night into Friday,
ending our period of wet weather. What guidance sources disagree
on is the character of the air mass behind the front. It will be
cooler, that's for sure. After all, we were near all time record
warmth for October ahead of it. However, just how cold is less
certain. Ensemble guidance varies largely by which parent model
system is being used. ECMWF guidance tends to be on the warmer 
end, with the core of the cold air pushing more toward New 
England. This leaves us cooler, but still near or even above 
normal for mid October. The GFS tends to be on the colder side, 
and the latest runs continue to come in even colder, sending the
core of the cold air right through the center of the country. 
The GFS actually latches on to Polar air and crashes it south 
all the way to the Gulf Coast. Under this colder scenario 
freezing temperatures are possible.

The uncertainty is largely driven by the intensity and 
amplitude of the trough driving this front and subsequently the 
trajectory of cold air behind it. Looking at the LREF cluster 
analysis, the warmer clusters contain almost no GEFS members and
feature 850mb temperatures this weekend as warm as +10C. The 
colder clusters contain almost no ENS members and feature 850mb 
temperatures as cold as -4C. The difference at the surface 
assuming full mixing is highs in the 70s vs highs in the low 
50s. And with the very low dewpoints being driven in by the 
colder guidance, overnight lows would have the potential to drop
below freezing on a clear, calm night behind the front. Even 
NBM is starting to show this with probability of temperatures 
dropping below freezing rising to 10-20 percent by Sunday 
morning area wide.

develops this morning dissipates with the rising sun, VFR flight
